content.overview: Traceability connects crop history to harvest, drying, cure/storage, packaging, samples and deviations. It enables investigations without relying on memory and allows affected scope to be identified when a problem appears.

vocabulary.definition: Ability to follow material identity, history and transitions through a process.
Recorded relationship between source material, splits, merges and downstream lots.
A documented departure from a defined process, condition or expected result.

sections.title: Stable IDs prevent history loss
sections.body: Use persistent lot and sample identifiers even when a commercial name or package format changes.

sections.title: Splits and merges need genealogy
sections.body: If one harvest becomes several drying/storage lots, or lots are combined, record those relationships explicitly.

sections.title: Process data should be attached to identity
sections.body: Drying dates, environmental trends, packaging and samples are useful only when they can be associated with the correct material.

workedExamples: If one drying rack experiences a humidity excursion, rack-to-lot mapping allows the potentially affected material to be scoped.
If two lots are blended without genealogy, later quality findings cannot be cleanly traced back.
commonMistakes: Using product names instead of stable IDs.
Keeping environmental records without batch association.
content.practicalApplication: Draw the genealogy of one example crop from harvest through drying, storage, package and test sample; ensure every transition has a timestamp and responsible record.
content.summary: Traceability turns post-harvest history into searchable evidence and limits the scope of uncertainty when problems occur.
